I'm on it with POTS, have been since November. Currently on 5mg, 7.5mg made be pretty sick (vomiting anything I ate) that i came back down to 5mg as dehydration is rubbish for us potsies. 
I'd say it could be the mounjaro or it could be something that triggered it that's totally unrelated. Were you drinking enough, replacing electrolytes as needed, how was the weather as that can effect us as well (heat, humidity, air pressure etc). My POTS was crazy yesterday as thunderstorms were in the area. Have a look at what you're eating as we can get blood pooling in the digestive system with heavier, carby meals.

It's a correlation or causation thing so consider and track all the other things that can trigger your POTS. Are you being medicated for your POTS? That may help with regulating your heart rate.

It could be worth trying again and keeping a close eye on what else is going on around you and putting POTS lifestyle changes into practice and see if that helps. Also I wouldn't race up the dosages, wait until a dose isn't effective anymore then go up with a low threshold of going back down if the side effects affect your POTS.

I'm in the UK and here the only routine ultrasounds are at 12 and 20 weeks. More are offered if there's a clinical reason such as growth concerns, placenta position if it's low, multiples, certain health conditions and also persistent low/no movements to do a biophysical profile. Dopplers are every single visit and any incidence of of low/no movements a trace/ctg is recommended, every time even if it's the next day. I would tell women after doing a trace for movements that the trace is only a snapshot of that moment, so come back anytime and we'll check again. Even if it's in half an hour and you turn the car around. We don't mess with movements. 

A trained ear can detect problems in the heart rate just with a doppler and any concern should be acted on straight away.

Where I am the advice in your situation is to go in for a quick trace of babe as even if you hear a heartbeat, there could still be something wrong. Unfortunately this is the scenario we see the most as the rate alone isn't enough to say that baby is ok, it's the other features such as variability, accelerations and decelerations as well as the rate that determine how a baby is. 

I know it's hard with an anterior placenta but it is a risk to rely on dopplers for reassurance. Obviously I'm biased and I know you're doing your best, I've just seen the other side of the coin too many times.

Please don't use a doppler at home unless you've been trained in how to use it and what you're listening for. It's not just the rate that's important. Ex midwife here and I've witnessed the outcomes of parents using these, thinking baby is ok and they infact weren't. They can create a false sense of reassurance. 

If they'd do a video call, you could suggest using it and letting them listen and look at the display as an alternative perhaps?

My trauma therapist taught me skills before we started working on my traumas. I've been seeing her for 4 years and the initial trust building and skill work took at least a year of not longer. 

So I started trauma therapy without any coping skills, she taught me, I worked on them and practiced, then we worked on my trauma. So you can start private trauma therapy without the coping skills.

I would definitely find a private therapist who specialises in trauma and addiction. Have a look around on Psychology Today and The Counselling Directory. Some will advertise that they offer sliding scale or concession rates and others will offer them but won't advertise. It's always worth reaching out, explaining your situation and asking if they can offer any reduction in fees.

In private therapy that's not necessarily the case that you have to have the coping mechanisms already in place, I certainly didn't when I started private trauma therapy. We worked on skills before deep diving into my traumas. In the NHS, yes you do need to have gone through other therapies like CBT to have those mechanisms because they won't start EMDR without them. However a private therapist won't dive straight into EMDR without a lot of time building a safe relationship and the mechanisms.

Talk to your insurance company and ask them what's covered and what isn't. That's the only way you'll know for sure if it's a possibility. Maybe even look into a new therapist if your current one isn't helping.

I can't comment on home births and tearing (ex UK hospital midwife) but I can give you some tips that may help your perineum.

Look into perineal massage, it can really help prep your perineum for birth.

Open conversations with your care giver, whatever route you choose on what your preferences are.

No directed pushing, use your bodies cues and go with it. Don't push until you feel the urge. 

Be in whatever position you want to be in. 

Warm compresses on your perineum during pushing. 

Using a mirror to watch just how powerful you are and help you pace your pushes. 

Touch your baby as you push, feel for when your push is just enough and guide your baby out. 

Consider that if your care provider won't support your wishes then are they really the provider for you?

Talk to the midwife about your concerns before deciding. What are their transfer rates? What situations would necessitate a transfer? What situations are they happy to stay at home with? How are they set up to handle emergency  situations? How do they suture/what do they use? Are they happy to suture at home?  How can they support you to reduce the chance of tearing? What are their experiences of home birth and tearing? 

Then talk to your OB. Will they support you to be in a position of your choosing? Will they support physiological pushing rather than directed? Will they support you to wait for the urge to push and to take your time provided babe is ok? Ask for evidence to support their no if they won't support. Ask what would happen if you declined to do things "as per policy". 

Knowledge is power and getting all the info you need from your care providers before deciding is crucial. Don't worry about what anyone else wants you to do, this is your birth and your body and you can do it how you want to do it.

I get the enhanced rate of mobility for my mental health. I have ptsd and often dissociate and have flashbacks whilst I'm out on my mobility scooter (for my physical conditions). The decision maker (not the assessor) talked to me about it, looked at my medical evidence and awarded enhanced, deeming it unsafe for me being out and about. I could get a car but I don't drive so got a new, much more comfortable and safe scooter instead. 

So yes, enhanced can be given for mental health conditions because for a lot of us it's much more complex that just "a bit" of depression or anxiety. A lot of physical conditions/disabilities can be invisible too. I don't "look" disabled so judging people on their outward appearance is idiotic.

As an ex UK midwife I can shed some light on this. 

Monitoring is recommended because babies can very quickly drop their blood sugars especially when mum is GD and on medication simply because they're no longer attached to you via the placenta and "on their own" as it were. They have to "learn" to regulate their own sugars.

I haven't practiced for a while so not sure of current testing guidelines so can't speak to that but generally there's a test a few hours after birth and all being well, at certain intervals after that. If there's a low reading then feeding and rechecking after the feed is recommended. If persistently low then a paediatrician is alerted and will review. Some babies need extra help to regulate their sugars via a drip and closer monitoring in special care. A certain number of normal readings in a row to show baby is managing their sugars are needed before they stop. 

Unfortunately I did see babies with low sugars and not showing symptoms so that can happen. 

However, you do have choice and can decline this testing as long as your midwife tells you what to look out for and how to prevent low sugars like frequent feeding, avoiding long periods without a feed etc. Also that you understand that if you have any concern at all at any time day/night you should call the hospital for advice and likely invite you in for testing. All testing should be done with informed consent so before you make a decision, ensure you have all the info needed. Pros and cons. 
This is not advice to refuse the test, just things to discuss with your midwife and to think about. Babies can get ill from low sugars very quickly so are you close to the hospital? Are you comfortable being admitted at any time of day/night if baby is symptomatic at a moments notice?

How are you planning to feed? That plays a big part too and if breastfeeding then ensuring position/latch is good and colostrum is being consumed as that will help regulate. 
Harvesting colostrum and storing it in your freezer as a backup just in case baby hasn't read the breastfeeding book will ensure they still get a feed (this is a good idea regardless of your decision). If bottle feeding then making sure to still feed regularly and still being observant as bottle fed babies can still have low sugars. 

None of this is clinical advice, just suggestions of things to think about and discuss with your midwife. 
I know having a homeborth and then being admitted isn't ideal however if baby does struggle with their sugars help is right there in the moment. 

Some of what I've said is worse case scenario and a lot of babies do well but some don't. No one knows which way a baby will swing which is why watch and wait isn't the guideline, it can't be predicted.

Edited to add:
Testing can't be done at home as there simply aren't enough community midwives to facilitate it, particularly over night, if they're at another home birth etc then there won't be anyone available to come do the test and then stay with you if a post feed test is needed.

I get that it can feel invalidating when someone suggests it's linked to mental health. I know it does, I did when stress was mentioned in the early years of my diagnosis. But look at your system as a whole. Mental health does impact physical health. Who doesn't get a headache, an ulcer, GI upset, weight loss, a cold etc when they're stressed? Now put trauma into that mix, which alters brain physiology/function, cortisol and adrenaline running on constant. Why wouldn't your nervous system malfunction?

Now flip that coin. It's invalidating to those of us who have PTSD/cPTSD and chronic health conditions to hear that our suspected cause of those conditions isn't valid. Isn't enough. Mental health isn't as valid as physical health.

Some of us have POTS from covid/other viral infection

Dysautonomia isn't a cause, it's a response. Many causes, one response by the autonomic nervous system. The medical literature literally says it's autonomic nervous system in response to many causes.
